summary: Re-plan of build case-onboarding to version 3, after the plan-verifier refuted v2 on 11 blockers and 11 warnings. All 22 blocker and warning ids are dispositioned: 9 blockers fixed in the plan body, 2 (B06, B07) shown by re-running the checkers to be no longer defects, 1 (B04) closed by a concurrent writer landing metadata-examples.md in admin/case-management-setup, 9 warnings fixed, 1 (W06) refuted with fixture evidence and its test removed instead of rescoped, and 1 (W11) confirmed as the CLI's write rather than the agent's. Running every checker the plan touches against throwaway fixtures surfaced 10 further defects the v2 verification did not raise — five checkers that fail on this build's correct artefacts, two that do not recurse, one that misparses AssignmentRules, one vacuous folder scan, and a dependency on a newly-blocked step that would have stranded three others. Shape: 5 milestones, 22 steps, 2 blocked (M3-S05 on deferred Q32-Q35; M5-S02 on four sandbox-strategy inputs that exist nowhere on file), 10 decisions, 28 assumptions, 18 fit-gap rows. validate exits 0 with 6 warnings, all of them the correct non-standard-argument-form notice; the two check_rtm warnings from v2 are cleared and no cross-referential-scope warning remains.
confidence_rationale: MEDIUM on three counts from this agent's own rubric: two of 22 steps are blocked (M3-S05, M5-S02), three decisions (D3, D4, D7) and D10 carry adr_required true with D10 resolved from a source_reference rather than a tree branch, and 25 blocking clarifications were deferred rather than answered at G1. Not LOW: 2 of 22 steps blocked is well under the quarter threshold, no two answers contradict each other on a decision the plan had to make, and validate exits 0 with no errors. Not HIGH, beyond the rubric: 14 checker tests were carried forward from v2 without a fixture run in this round, and this round found that a v2-verified description was wrong more often than it was right.

assumptions.text: No automation overwrites a value a human has already set: the stamping flow writes only into null fields, and the support manager repairs a wrong automation result by hand.
assumptions.because: Q14 was deferred; writing only into nulls is the option that cannot destroy an agent's work. (source: deferred clarification Q14)

assumptions.text: The org is on Lightning Threading (Email-to-Case thread identifier in the headers), and every customer-facing template still carries the visible thread token as a belt-and-braces fallback.

decisions.decision: Stamp Case.EntitlementId, Case.BusinessHoursId and the Priority default in one before-save record-triggered Flow rather than in Apex or an after-save Flow.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q2. Does the logic run in under ~10s and touch only fields on the record itself?
    ├── Yes, but the field is OwnerId (or an acknowledgement, or an SLA
    │        clock) on a Case or a Lead                               → Q13
    ├── Yes  → Before-save record-triggered Flow
    └── No   → Q3
decisions.rationale: All three writes land on the triggering Case and the Account/Entitlement reads are lookups, not DML, so Q1's record-change branch reaches Q2. Q2's first branch redirects the Case-specific engine choices to Q13, and this plan takes that redirect elsewhere: the owner write is D3 (Q13), the acknowledgement is the auto-response rule in M3-S04 (Q13), and the SLA engine itself is the entitlement process in M4-S02 (Q15). What is left at Q2's plain 'Yes' leaf is exactly this step — the same-record field write that puts the Case into that engine. The Q15 leaf note is why the step has to exist at all: 'neither Email-to-Case nor Web-to-Case supplies an entitlement, so a case-intake design that stops at the channel tracks nothing until something assigns one.'
alternatives_rejected: three separate flows, one per field
decisions.consequences: No Apex means no coverage gate and no deploy-time test dependency, but also no custom exception handling: a Case whose Account has no entitlement must fall through to a documented default rather than throw (Q48).

decisions.decision: The stamping flow is before-save, not after-save: the Account and Entitlement lookups are read-only Get Records, which a before-save flow supports.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q3. Do you need any DML, an Action/callout, or an email — anything beyond
    writing fields on the triggering record?
    ├── No   → Before-Save record-triggered flow. Its element set is
                Assignment, Decision, Get Records, Loop — so a read-only
                cross-object lookup is fine here; a write is not.
decisions.rationale: Q1 'record INSERT or UPDATE' → Q2 'only set fields on the SAME record' → Q3 'no DML, no action, no email' → before-save. The branch text settles the one thing that looked like an obstacle: the cross-object read is allowed.
decisions.consequences: The customer acknowledgement (an email) cannot live in this flow; it stays in the auto-response rule (M3-S04), which is what Q63 asked for anyway.

decisions.decision: Case ownership at creation is set by Case Assignment Rules, and the assignment rule is the sole authoritative OwnerId writer at create time.
decisions.rationale: automation-selection Q2's first branch redirects an OwnerId write on a Case to Q13, and Q13's first leaf is this decision verbatim: the first owner is a function of field values (Origin, Account support tier) held in an ordered criteria table. The tree's own 'Why each leaf' note adds the reason a Flow is wrong here: assignment rules run at save-order position 9, after all after triggers and before after-save record-triggered flows at position 14, so a before-save Flow that sets OwnerId is simply overwritten. skills/admin/assignment-rules/references/routing-selector.md row 1 says the same thing and is recorded as the corroborating source.
alternatives_rejected: Omni-Channel alone with no queue-landing rule
decisions.consequences: Two by-design post-save OwnerId writers remain (Omni-Channel push in M3-S05 and the escalation rule in M4-S04). Q27 already flagged this; owner-writer-map.md in M3-S04 is the artefact that has to reconcile all three.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q13. Which native rule engine on Case or Lead owns this write?
     ├── The first owner comes from an ordered criteria table
     │   of field values                                          → Assignment Rules · `admin/assignment-rules`

decisions.decision: Tier 1 receives pushed work through queue-based Omni-Channel granted by profile; Tier 2 and Billing pull from queue list views.
decisions.rationale: Q13's second leaf is the decision: the question is who is free, not which team, and the tree's 'Why each leaf' note states that Omni-Channel sits on top of the assignment rule rather than instead of it — the rule lands the Case in the queue, Omni-Channel pushes it to an agent. That settles the mechanism. It does not settle the configuration: Q32-Q35 (objects pushed and capacity release, capacity model and weight, routing model and tie-breaker, push timeout) were all deferred at G1 and no cited skill documents a default for three of the four, so M3-S05 is written blocked rather than carrying invented numbers.
alternatives_rejected: Skills-based routing (Q37: no skill dimension in the requirement)
Per-user presence assignment (Q36: Tier 1 membership changes monthly)
decisions.consequences: Omni-Channel writes OwnerId after save, which is the second of the three owner writers D3 has to reconcile. M3-S05 is blocked on Q32-Q35, so nothing in this build configures the push half; Tier 1 works the Tier 1 General queue list view produced by M5-S01 until those four questions are answered.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q13. Which native rule engine on Case or Lead owns this write?
     ├── The record is already in a queue and must reach whichever
     │   agent is online and under capacity                       → Omni-Channel · `admin/omni-channel-routing-setup`

decisions.decision: Case org-wide default stays Private and Tier 2 reaches Support cases through a criteria-based sharing rule on record type; nothing extends Billing cases to Tier 1.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q3. Can the access be described by "anyone who matches criteria X should see records matching criteria Y"?
    ├── Yes, criteria are on the record itself          → Criteria-Based Sharing Rule
decisions.rationale: Q1 'Private → Q2'; the three teams are peers, not a hierarchy, so Q2's 'No' branch leads to Q3; the access is exactly 'the Tier 2 group should see cases whose RecordType is Support', and RecordTypeId is on the record itself.
decisions.consequences: Deferred Q13 asked whether the Billing restriction is record-level or field-level. The plan takes the record-level (more restrictive) reading as assumption A1. If the answer turns out to be field-level masking, M2-S05 is re-planned, not patched.

decisions.decision: The website form posts to native Web-to-Case; no middleware, no Bulk API and no custom REST endpoint is introduced.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q14. Which intake channel creates the Case?
     ├── Customer email to a monitored routing address            → Email-to-Case · `admin/email-to-case-configuration`
     ├── An HTML form posted from a public website                → Web-to-Case · `admin/case-management-setup`
decisions.rationale: Q13's fourth leaf ('The record arrives from an inbound intake channel') routes to Q14, whose second leaf is native Web-to-Case for an HTML form posted from a public website and whose first is Email-to-Case for a monitored routing address. That is the positive half of this decision, and it is what the v1 plan was missing. integration-pattern-selection Q5 was also read and settles the negative half by volume: 60 web submissions plus 400 emails a day sit in its lowest band, so Bulk API 2.0 and an iPaaS are ruled out. The tree's Q14 'Why each leaf' note adds the constraint the plan follows in M3-S03 and M3-S04: ownership belongs in the assignment rule reading Case.Origin per address, not in the channel's own owner field.
decisions.consequences: Q66 left open whether the form posts directly or through middleware. If middleware turns out to sit in front, the Origin stamping in M3-S03 and the assignment criteria in M3-S04 both change. Assumption A26 is not recorded because Q66 is answered — the answer itself says 'confirm', so the confirmation is a manual test on M3-S03.

decisions.decision: The 8-business-hour Tier 2 handoff is a Case Escalation Rule, not a scheduled Flow or a time-based Apex job.
decisions.rationale: Q13's fifth leaf ('Something must happen because time has passed') routes to Q15, whose first leaf is this decision: re-route or notify when an open Case ages past a threshold. The tree's 'Why each leaf' note is the reason a scheduled Flow is wrong: escalation rules run at save-order position 12 and then on their own timer against business hours, and a polling Flow 'will not honour the per-entry businessHoursSource or the escalationStartTime choice between case creation and last modification' — both of which Q42 and Q43 answered explicitly. automation-selection Q10 and async-selection were both read and route only between Batch, Queueable and Schedule-triggered Flow, all of which re-implement the engine.
alternatives_rejected: After-save Flow with a scheduled path
decisions.consequences: The escalation engine batches, so the 480-minute threshold is not a to-the-second promise (Q46 asked for headroom to be agreed). The rule also writes OwnerId, which is the third owner writer D3 has to reconcile.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q15. What does the passage of time have to do?
     ├── Re-route or notify when an open Case ages past a
     │   threshold                                                → Escalation Rules · `admin/escalation-rules`

decisions.decision: Nothing in this build runs asynchronously: no @future, no Queueable, no Batch, no Schedulable and no Platform Event.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q1. How many records / how long?
    ├── < 2,000 records, < 60s          → Q2
    ├── 2k – 50k, < 5 min                → Q5 (Queueable)
    ├── > 50k OR > 5 min                 → Q8 (Batch Apex)
    └── Truly massive, one-off ETL       → Bulk API 2.0 (async SOQL / external job)
decisions.rationale: The worst case anyone described is the daily email peak of ~400 cases (Q15), and those arrive as individual API inserts, never as one 2,000-record transaction. Q1's first band applies and the tree never reaches an async tier.
decisions.consequences: Every automation in the plan runs inside the creating transaction, so the before-save flow in M4-S03 is on the critical path of every intake. If volume grows past the Q1 first band, this decision is the one to revisit.

decisions.decision: Case is treated as an ordinary object: no skinny table, no custom index request and no archival design in this phase.
decisions.branch_quote:
Q10. What stage of LDV are you in?
    ├── Designing a new high-volume object           → architect/large-data-volume-architecture (skinny + indexes from day one)
decisions.rationale: The tree was entered because the requirement names a volume (Q15: ~480 cases/day). Q1's symptom router has no branch for a greenfield design with no reported symptom, so Q10's design-stage branch is the only reachable entry. ~480/day is roughly 175k Cases a year, well below the thresholds that branch exists for, so the answer is 'not this'.
alternatives_rejected: Skinny table on Case from day one
Big Object archival of closed cases
decisions.consequences: The escalation monitoring report (M5-S01) and the queue list views (M5-S01) are unindexed selective queries today. Q76 already asked which acceptance criteria depend on volume; if the report degrades, this decision is where the revisit starts.

decisions.decision: Mark the First Response milestone complete with an after-update Apex trigger on Case that stamps CaseMilestone.CompletionDate, not with entitlement-process completion criteria and not with a Flow.
decisions.rationale: automation-selection was read end to end before this was called treeless. Q2's first branch sends an SLA clock on a Case to Q13, and Q13's fifth leaf sends it to Q15, whose second leaf selects Entitlement milestones as the engine — that is D-level ground for M4-S02 and nothing more; no leaf in Q13, Q14 or Q15 says who writes CompletionDate. Q3's Apex list does not name it either. The skill is the source: skills/admin/entitlements-and-milestones/references/gotchas.md gotcha 8 states that a milestone stays open until something writes CompletionDate and that the mechanism must ship with the process, and references/metadata-examples.md § 9 shows CaseMilestone supports only update() with CompletionDate and StartDate as its two updateable fields. skills/apex/entitlement-apex-hooks declares exactly this artefact as its output — an after-update trigger on Case that writes CompletionDate to open CaseMilestone records, plus its test class — so the Apex path is the one the library documents end to end. The declarative alternative is not chosen because no cited reference documents an EntitlementProcess completion-criteria element; milestoneCriteriaFilterItems is a start criterion (api_meta.txt:59198-59201), not a completion one.
alternatives_rejected: Satisfiable completion criteria on the entitlement process (no completion-criteria element is documented in the skill's metadata reference)

A record-triggered Flow stamping CompletionDate directly (metadata-examples § 9 documents the Flow path as an invocable wrapper around this same Apex, so it adds a component without removing the Apex)
Leaving completion manual (gotcha 8: every first-response milestone then reports violated on cases the agent demonstrably answered)
decisions.consequences: This is the only Apex in the build, so M4-S05 is the only step under the 75% coverage gate and the only one whose artefacts a deploy will compile. Violation polling is deliberately not built: the same skill's MilestoneViolationScheduler is Schedulable, which D8 rules out for this phase.
